pairs.source_text: quippe in regiones quattuordecim Romam dividitur, quarum quattuor integrae manebant, tres solo tenus deiectae, septem reliquis pauca tectorum vestigia supererant, lacera et semusta.
pairs.question: Quot ex quattuordecim urbis Romae regionibus post magnum incendium integrae manserunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Of the fourteen regions of the city of Rome, how many remained intact after the great fire, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: The precise toll of the Great Fire of AD 64. Anchored to Rome's fourteen regiones + the Neronian fire; single number, supported verbatim by 'quarum quattuor integrae manebant'. Direct question, indicative manserunt, with 'ut Tacitus tradit' as parenthetical frame. Closed-book: the breakdown of Rome's regions after the fire is a specific, oft-cited fact.

pairs.source_text: quippe in regiones quattuordecim Romam dividitur, quarum quattuor integrae manebant, tres solo tenus deiectae, septem reliquis pauca tectorum vestigia supererant, lacera et semusta.
pairs.question: Quot ex quattuordecim Romae regionibus magno illo incendio solo tenus deiectae sunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: How many of Rome's fourteen regions were razed to the ground by that great fire, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: From the same regio breakdown of the Great Fire. Anchored to Rome's fourteen regiones + the Neronian fire; single number, supported verbatim by 'tres solo tenus deiectae'. Direct question, indicative deiectae sunt. Closed-book number fact about the fire's destruction.

pairs.source_text: Sexto demum die apud imas Esquilias finis incendio factus, prorutis per immensum aedificiis, ut continuae violentiae campus et velut vacuum caelum occurreret.
pairs.question: Quoto die magnum urbis Romae incendium apud imas Esquilias finem habuit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: On what day did the great fire of Rome come to an end at the lower Esquiline, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the Neronian fire + the lower Esquiline; single ordinal, supported verbatim by 'Sexto demum die apud imas Esquilias finis incendio factus'. Direct question, indicative habuit. Closed-book number fact about the duration of the Great Fire (the fire later flared again, but Tacitus marks this first end on the sixth day).

pairs.source_text: Sed non ope humana, non largitionibus principis aut deum placamentis decedebat infamia, quin iussum incendium crederetur. ergo abolendo rumori Nero subdidit reos et quaesitissimis poenis adfecit, quos per flagitia invisos vulgus Chrestianos appellabat.
pairs.question: Quos Nero, ut rumorem de incendio urbis aboleret, reos subdidit et quaesitissimis poenis adfecit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Nero put up as culprits and punish with the most refined penalties, in order to dispel the rumor about the fire of the city, according to Tacitus?
pairs.answer_en: Those whom the crowd called Chrestiani (the Christians).
pairs.derivation: The famous passage on Nero's persecution. Anchored to Nero + the fire of Rome; the answer (the Christians) is supported verbatim by 'subdidit reos ... quos per flagitia invisos vulgus Chrestianos appellabat'. Purpose clause 'ut ... aboleret' (subjunctive), main verb subdidit indicative. Closed-book: that Nero blamed the Christians for the Great Fire is among the most-cited facts of his reign.

pairs.source_text: auctor nominis eius Christus Tibero imperitante per procuratorem Pontium Pilatum supplicio adfectus erat
pairs.question: Quem auctorem nominis Christianorum (Chrestianorum) fuisse Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whom does Tacitus report to have been the originator of the name of the Christians?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to the Christians + the originator of their name; single named person, supported verbatim by 'auctor nominis eius Christus ...'. Indirect statement (Christum ... fuisse) governed by tradit. Closed-book: Tacitus's identification of Christus as the founder is one of the most-quoted lines in classical literature.

pairs.source_text: auctor nominis eius Christus Tibero imperitante per procuratorem Pontium Pilatum supplicio adfectus erat
pairs.question: Quo principe imperante et per quem procuratorem Christum supplicio adfectum esse Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Under which emperor and by which procurator does Tacitus report that Christ was executed?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Christus; two named entities (the emperor Tiberius, the procurator Pontius Pilatus), both supported verbatim by 'Tibero imperitante per procuratorem Pontium Pilatum supplicio adfectus erat' (the text reads 'Tibero'). Indirect statement (Christum ... adfectum esse) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the execution of Christ by Pilate under Tiberius is among the most famous facts derivable from Tacitus.

pairs.source_text: coepta simul et aucta coniuratione, in quam certatim nomina dederant senatores eques miles, feminae etiam, cum odio Neronis, tum favore in C. Pisonem. is Calpurnio genere ortus ac multas insignesque familias paterna nobilitate complexus, claro apud vulgum rumore erat
pairs.question: Quem coniurati, qui adversus Neronem coierant, favore suo prosequebantur, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did the conspirators who had banded together against Nero favor, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: The Pisonian conspiracy of AD 65. Anchored to the conspiracy against Nero; single named person, supported verbatim by 'favore in C. Pisonem' and 'is Calpurnio genere ortus'. Direct question, indicative prosequebantur. Closed-book: the conspiracy is named after C. Calpurnius Piso, its figurehead.

pairs.source_text: Sequitur caedes Annaei Senecae, laetissima principi, non quia coniurationis manifestum compererat, sed ut ferro grassaretur, quando venenum non processerat.
pairs.question: Quem philosophum, Neronis quondam praeceptorem, mori coactum Tacitus inter coniurationis Pisonianae caedes refert?
pairs.question_en: Which philosopher, once Nero's tutor, does Tacitus report to have been forced to die among the killings of the Pisonian conspiracy?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Nero's tutor + the Pisonian conspiracy; single named person, supported verbatim by 'Sequitur caedes Annaei Senecae'. That Seneca was Nero's praeceptor is reinforced at 15.62 ('educatoris praeceptorisque necem'). Indirect statement (Senecam ... coactum [esse]) governed by refert. Closed-book: Seneca as Nero's tutor and his forced death are stock facts.

pairs.source_text: post quae eodem ictu brachia ferro exsolvunt. Seneca, quoniam senile corpus et parco victu tenuatum lenta effugia sanguini praebebat, crurum quoque et poplitum venas abrumpit
pairs.question: Quo modo Seneca, Neronis iussu, mori coactus est, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: By what means was Seneca compelled to die at Nero's command, according to Tacitus?
pairs.answer_en: By cutting open his veins with a blade.
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Seneca + his forced death; the method (opening the veins) is supported verbatim by 'brachia ferro exsolvunt' and 'crurum quoque et poplitum venas abrumpit'. Direct question, indicative coactus est. Closed-book: Seneca's death by opening his veins is among the most famous suicides in Roman history.

pairs.source_text: scribitur tetrarchis ac regibus praefectisque et procuratoribus et qui praetorum finitimas provincias regebant, iussis Corbulonis obsequi, in tantum ferme modum aucta potestate, quem populus Romanus Cn. Pompeio bellum piraticum gesturo dederat.
pairs.question: Cuius imperatoris potestati, olim bello piratico gerendo datae, Corbulonis adversus Parthos potestatem Tacitus comparat?
pairs.question_en: To the power of which commander, once granted for waging the war against the pirates, does Tacitus compare Corbulo's power against the Parthians?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Corbulo + the Parthian command + the pirate war; single named person, supported verbatim by 'in tantum ferme modum aucta potestate, quem populus Romanus Cn. Pompeio bellum piraticum gesturo dederat'. Direct question, indicative comparat. Closed-book: Pompey's extraordinary command against the pirates is a stock fact, here the measure of Corbulo's authority.

pairs.source_text: medio tribunal sedem curulem et sedes effigiem Neronis sustinebat. ad quam progressus Tiridates, caesis ex more victimis, sublatum capiti diadema imagini subiecit, magnis apud cunctos animorum motibus
pairs.question: Cuius imagini Tiridates, Vologaesis Parthorum regis frater, diadema de capite sublatum subiecit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Before whose image did Tiridates, brother of Vologaeses king of the Parthians, place the diadem taken from his head, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: The famous submission of Tiridates. Anchored to Tiridates + Vologaeses; single named person (Nero), supported verbatim by 'sedes effigiem Neronis sustinebat. ad quam progressus Tiridates ... diadema imagini subiecit'. Direct question, indicative subiecit. Closed-book: Tiridates laying his diadem before Nero's image (prelude to his later coronation at Rome) is a well-known episode.

pairs.source_text: Memmio Regulo et Verginio Rufo consulibus natam sibi ex Poppaea filiam Nero ultra mortale gaudium accepit appelavitque Augustam, dato et Poppaea eodem cognomento. locus puerperio colonia Antium fuit, ubi ipse generatus erat.
pairs.question: In qua colonia natum esse Neronem ipsum Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: In which colony does Tacitus report that Nero himself was born?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Nero; single named place, supported by 'locus puerperio colonia Antium fuit, ubi ipse generatus erat' (ipse = Nero, just named). Indirect statement (Neronem natum esse) governed by tradit. Closed-book: Nero's birth at Antium is a stock biographical fact.

pairs.source_text: et motu terrae celebre Campaniae oppidum Pompei magna ex parte proruit; defunctaque virgo Vestalis Laelia, in cuius locum Cornelia ex familia Cossorum capta est.
pairs.question: Quod celebre Campaniae oppidum motu terrae magna ex parte prorutum esse Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which famous town of Campania does Tacitus report to have largely collapsed in an earthquake?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Campania + the earthquake; single named place, supported verbatim by 'celebre Campaniae oppidum Pompei magna ex parte proruit'. Indirect statement (oppidum ... prorutum esse) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the earthquake that struck Pompeii (the great Campanian quake under Nero) is a documented event.

pairs.source_text: Ceterum Nero usus est patriae ruinis exstruxitque domum, in qua haud proinde gemmae et aurum miraculo essent, solita pridem et luxu vulgata, quam arva et stagna et in modum solitudinem hinc silvae, inde aperta spatia et prospetus, magistris et machinatoribus Severo et Celere, quibus ingenium et audacia erat etiam, quae natura denegavisset, per artem temptare et viribus principis inludere.
pairs.question: Quos magistros et machinatores adhibuit Nero in exstruenda domo, quam post incendium urbis ruinis aedificavit, ut Tacitus tradit?
pairs.question_en: Which architects and engineers did Nero employ in building the house that he constructed from the ruins of the city after the fire, according to Tacitus?
pairs.derivation: Anchored to Nero + the palace built after the fire (the Domus Aurea); two named persons, supported verbatim by 'magistris et machinatoribus Severo et Celere'. Direct question, indicative adhibuit. Closed-book: Severus and Celer are the recorded architects/engineers of Nero's new palace.
